Lead story · AI · Photo editing · 1 Nov

Adobe is teaching AI to edit like a Photoshop pro

Adobe Research and UC San Diego have built EditAgent, an AI system that edits photos the way an experienced retoucher works: pick the right tool for each step, try options side by side, then check the result with real numbers instead of just eyeballing it.

The problem. Today's AI editing agents usually split a request into steps, retry the same editor when a step fails, and let another model judge the output by looking at it. In Adobe's test of 600 edits, rated blind by five professionals, a general-purpose editor gave no usable result 42.7% of the time. Retrying the same editor barely helped.

The fix: more tools, side by side. Specialist tools for jobs like sharpening, rotating and zooming solved about two-thirds of those failures. And generating several fresh options from the original image beat fixing one image again and again, because small errors pile up with each round. Professionals preferred the parallel versions in 78.5% of the comparisons where they picked a side.

Checking with numbers. For each option, the judging model gets a close-up of the edited area, a map of what changed and measured brightness and colour values. In one example, a "gently brighten" request made the general editor overexpose the photo and warm the colours, and the numbers caught it. With this record, ordinary language models picked a usable result 81.3% of the time, ahead of a model trained only for judging (74.8%).

The catch. The agent needs about ten times the computing power of a single editor. But because it keeps only verified results, it produced about 26,000 clean training examples that made other editors better. Adobe added AI agents to Photoshop, Premiere and other Creative Cloud apps in June as a public beta, so this research points straight at the tools you use.

What this means for you

This is how good retouchers already work: compare options against the original, zoom in, and check the histogram before you say "done". Make it your habit with AI too. Generate two or three variants from the untouched original instead of fixing one image five times, and check every AI edit at 100% zoom and with the Info panel open. Your eye plus measurement is still the quality control clients pay for.

AI Desk

OpenAI · 1 Nov

ChatGPT moves to one shared token budget

From December, ChatGPT Plus, Pro and Business plans will share a single token budget across ChatGPT and Codex, The Decoder reports. Heavier tasks use the budget faster; when it runs out you wait for a reset, upgrade or buy credits. If you use ChatGPT for image and layout work, keep an eye on the balance in Settings.

Google · 1 Nov

A video assistant that knows when to speak

Researchers from Google, Stanford, Oxford and others built StreamVibe, an assistant that watches a task like cooking and decides every second whether to stay quiet or help. They report 10.7% better timing and quality than other models, but all tested models still lose track over long sessions. A real UX lesson: helpful means not interrupting.

Anthropic · 31 Oct

Hidden watermarks spread to more AI text

Anthropic is adding its invisible text watermark, a pattern in word choice, to four more Claude models. On two older models it only works at default settings, so a small tweak removes it. For copywriters and content teams: AI-written text is becoming traceable, so disclose AI use honestly.

Prompt of the day · Test it, score it, then redesign it

The Galli Cup Night Poster

Winter evenings mean tennis-ball cricket under tube lights in every lane. Today's brief is a sports event poster for "GALLI CUP 2026", an invented lane tournament in Thane. Cricket is hard for AI: stumps, bails, a seamed ball and a correct batting grip all break easily.

Score: 0 / 5

Student task: use the AI image only for the night mood and the action pose. Rebuild the title in Illustrator or Figma with a condensed sans, add the Devanagari line yourself, and make a 9:16 story version where the date sits in the bottom third.

Version 1 · Any tool
Portrait 2:3 sports event poster for "GALLI CUP 2026", an invented night cricket tournament in a narrow Thane lane. A young batter in a plain white T-shirt plays a straight drive, holding one bat with both hands. One yellow tennis ball with tape, mid-air. Behind: exactly 3 wooden stumps with 2 bails, chalk crease on the road. Exactly 4 tube lights on the building walls, warm glow, moths, chawl balconies. Top: "GALLI CUP 2026" in bold condensed capitals. Below it: "गल्ली कप". Bottom: "SAT 14 NOV · 7 PM". No logos, no other text.

Why it works: every count, word and position is fixed, so each of the five checks has one clear right answer.

Version 2 · Midjourney V8
night street cricket in a narrow Indian chawl lane, young batter mid straight drive, taped tennis ball in the air, three wooden stumps with two bails, chalk crease on wet road, four warm tube lights on old walls, moths, balconies with laundry, low angle, cinematic sports poster, empty dark sky at top for title --ar 2:3 --v 8 --style raw --stylize 150 --no text, logo, watermark

V8 tip: ask for empty sky and no text. Let Midjourney handle light and motion, then set the title and date yourself.

Version 3 · Nano Banana
Step 1: Create a 2:3 night photo of tennis-ball cricket in a narrow Thane chawl lane. One batter plays a straight drive, holding one bat with both hands. Exactly 3 stumps with 2 bails behind him. Exactly 4 tube lights on the walls. Leave the top quarter as dark sky.

Step 2 (same chat): Keep the scene exactly the same. In the dark sky add "GALLI CUP 2026" in bold condensed white capitals and "गल्ली कप" below it. At the bottom add "SAT 14 NOV · 7 PM". Change nothing else.

What you are testing: whether adding text in step 2 changes the stump count, adds a second ball or breaks the Devanagari.

Version 4 · ChatGPT
Create a 2:3 poster for "GALLI CUP 2026", an invented night lane-cricket tournament in Thane.

Layout, top to bottom:
1. "GALLI CUP 2026" in bold condensed capitals
2. "गल्ली कप" in Devanagari
3. Photo: one batter, straight drive, one taped tennis ball, exactly 3 stumps with 2 bails, exactly 4 tube lights
4. "SAT 14 NOV · 7 PM" at the bottom

No people other than the batter, no logos, no other text.

Tip: if the bails are missing, reply "fix only the stumps, keep everything else". Then ask for a 9:16 story crop.

Graphic Design

Identity · 1 Nov

A bistro brand tilted like a shipyard ramp

Werf is a bar and bistro inside a working Rotterdam shipyard. andstudio built its identity on the 20-degree angle of the yard's launch ramps: huge slanted display type, small monospaced "paperwork" type, a steel menu held by hex bolts, and a bill written like a restoration report. Seasonal menu colours follow whichever ship is docked.

Rebrand · 1 Nov

Pink, not navy, for a maritime brand

HOW+HOW skipped the usual navy and white. Bristol Dockyards now uses a pink taken from Bristol's terraced houses, torn-paper collages from its archive, a heavy block wordmark and a classic serif for the story lines. The studio reports online conversion more than tripled after the relaunch.

Branding · 1 Nov

Brands are making video games again

Wendy's has revealed WendyQuest, a pixel-art, turn-based adventure heading to Steam, made by an indie studio in Canada. Creative Bloq notes gamers mostly praise how good it looks, and traces the idea back to cult hits like Pepsiman (1999) and 7 Up's Cool Spot (1993). Brand worlds are becoming playable spaces.

UI / UX

Messaging · 2 Nov

WhatsApp underlines what you can act on

WhatsApp now spots phone numbers, dates, addresses and emails in chats and marks them with a dotted underline. Tap it to call, add to contacts or calendar, create an event or open maps. The sheet shows the exact text detected, detection runs on the phone, and a small "useful / not useful" prompt collects feedback.

Video · 1 Nov

YouTube moves the Subscriptions tab

YouTube's new home screen drops the Subscriptions tab from the bottom bar; a Plus button sits where thumbs used to go. Subscriptions now live in a "Subs" section at the top of Home, without the old filters, Android Authority reports. Moving a habit-forming button breaks muscle memory, even when the feature still exists.

Fintech · 30 Oct

A banking app that doesn't look like a spreadsheet

Cuberto designed Wickret, a fee-free mobile bank, with Montserrat type, pastel bento cards, colour-coded card carousels and small illustrated keys and money bags. The idea: show balances at a glance with no nested menus, and add warmth so a money app feels friendly as well as trustworthy.

Student Corner

Entrance exams · Deadline

NIFT 2027 forms close on 16 November

The NIFT entrance exam application window runs until 16 November. A late fee of ₹5,000 applies from 17 to 21 November. The written exam is on 10 January 2027. NID DAT forms close on 30 November. Start your portfolio and sketch practice now, not after the forms.

Career · 30 Oct

Your edge in the AI age: curiosity

Writing in PRINT after Toronto's DesignThinkers conference, a New York-based designer argues that AI makes making images easy, so the real skill is asking better questions: what is worth making, whose view is missing, and does it communicate? Trends travel fast, and AI spreads them faster. Research makes work your own.

Design psychology term of the day

Signifier

A signifier is a visible clue that tells people what they can do and where. The term comes from Don Norman. WhatsApp's dotted underline is a perfect example: it quietly says "you can tap this" without a button or a label.

Try it: open one screen you designed and list every tappable item. If any of them has no visual clue (colour, underline, icon or shape), add one and test it on a friend.
